## ARGUMENT

### The officers unlawfully prolonged the traffic stop beyond the time reasonably required to complete its mission, without reasonable suspicion.

#### A. A traffic stop may last only as long as needed to address the traffic violation.

A traffic stop is a seizure under the Fourth Amendment and is analyzed under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1 (1968). *United States v. Karam*, 496 F.3d 1157, 1161 (10th Cir. 2007). The inquiry has two parts: whether the stop was justified at its inception, and whether the officer's actions were reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified the stop. *United States v. West*, 219 F.3d 1171, 1176 (10th Cir. 2000); *United States v. Wood*, 106 F.3d 942, 945 (10th Cir. 1997). Only the second part is at issue here.

The Supreme Court has made clear that "a police stop exceeding the time needed to handle the matter for which the stop was made violates the Constitution's shield against unreasonable seizures." *Rodriguez v. United States*, 575 U.S. 348, 350 (2015). Authority for the seizure "ends when tasks tied to the traffic infraction are—or reasonably should have been—completed." *Id.* at 354. Those tasks include checking the driver's license, determining whether there are outstanding warrants, and inspecting registration and proof of insurance. *Id.* at 355. Unrelated inquiries are not part of the stop's mission, and an officer may not prolong the stop to pursue them absent reasonable suspicion. *Id.* at 355–57.

The Tenth Circuit has long applied the same rule. An officer may request a driver's license and registration, run a computer check, and issue a citation. *United States v. Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d 1345, 1349 (10th Cir. 1998). Once those tasks are done, the driver must be allowed to proceed. *Id.*; *West*, 219 F.3d at 1176. Continued detention is permitted only if the driver consents or the officer has "an objectively reasonable and articulable suspicion that illegal activity has occurred or is occurring." *Wood*, 106 F.3d at 946; *see also* *Karam*, 496 F.3d at 1161–62.

#### B. Reasonable suspicion must rest on particularized facts, not a hunch.

Reasonable suspicion requires "a particularized and objective basis" for suspecting criminal activity. *United States v. Simpson*, 609 F.3d 1140, 1146 (10th Cir. 2010). An officer's "inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or 'hunch'" is not enough. *Terry*, 392 U.S. at 27. The Tenth Circuit has repeatedly refused to find reasonable suspicion where the government relied on facts that are consistent with innocent travel and that describe a large category of law-abiding motorists. *See* *Wood*, 106 F.3d at 948; *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1350–51; *West*, 219 F.3d at 1179. Nervousness, standing alone, is of limited significance. *Wood*, 106 F.3d at 948. The same is true of a driver's reasonable explanation of travel plans that the officer simply declines to credit. *See* *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1350–51.

The government bears the burden of establishing that the extended detention was justified. *See* *United States v. Santos*, 403 F.3d 1120, 1125 (10th Cir. 2005). Its justification is measured by what the officers actually knew when the stop was prolonged, not by information gathered afterward through the very detention under challenge. *See* *Wood*, 106 F.3d at 948.

#### C. The officers prolonged the stop without reasonable suspicion.

Here, the purpose of the stop was [describe the violation]. By [time], the officers had [verified the license, registration, and insurance; completed warrant checks]. At that point, the tasks tied to the infraction were, or reasonably should have been, complete. *Rodriguez*, 575 U.S. at 354. Instead of issuing the citation and releasing Appellant, the officers [describe the delay, such as waiting for a canine unit, continuing unrelated questioning, or retaining documents]. That conduct added [number] minutes to the stop and served no purpose related to the traffic violation. *See id.* at 355–57.

The government cannot justify the extension by pointing to [list the facts the government relied on, such as nervousness, travel itinerary, or the vehicle's origin]. Taken individually or together, these factors describe innocent behavior common among ordinary motorists, and they did not supply a particularized basis for suspecting criminal activity. *See* *Wood*, 106 F.3d at 948; *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1350–51; *West*, 219 F.3d at 1179. Nor did Appellant consent to continued detention. *See* *Karam*, 496 F.3d at 1162.

Because the officers lacked reasonable suspicion when the stop's lawful mission ended, the continued detention was an unreasonable seizure. The evidence obtained as a result of it must be suppressed as fruit of the unlawful seizure, and the district court erred in holding otherwise. *See* *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1351–52.
